name: The Dilbert Principle
statement: Companies promote their least competent people to management, to keep them out of the real work.
statementAccent: to keep them out of the real work
meaning: A satirical management idea holding that companies tend to promote their least competent employees into management, especially middle management, so as to move them out of the workflow where they can do the least damage to the actual productive work. The premise is cynical: that the real work is done by the lower ranks, and management is where the incompetent are parked.
mechanism: Where more earnest theories imagine promotion as a reward for competence, the Dilbert principle imagines it as a form of quarantine. The incompetent are not elevated because they did well; they are elevated to get them away from work that matters. It is deliberately provocative, distilling a jaundiced view of corporate life into a single rule, and it works by inverting the flattering assumption that organisations move their best people up.

examples.text: The idea is voiced within the Dilbert strip itself, in the mock wisdom that leadership is nature's way of removing morons from the productive flow.
The 1996 book skewers meaningless memos, jargon, pointy-haired bosses, and pseudo-productivity — the whole texture of late-twentieth-century office life the principle caricatures.

A tongue-in-cheek 2010 modelling study, which won an Ig Nobel, argued organisations would do better promoting people at random than by apparent merit — adjacent in spirit, though aimed at the Peter principle.

variants.name: The Peter principle
variants.text: The earlier, more earnest idea that employees are promoted on competence until they reach a role they cannot do; the Dilbert principle is its cynical inversion, promoting the incompetent first and on purpose.

variants.name: Putt's Law
variants.text: An antecedent aphorism that technology is dominated by those who manage what they do not understand, part of the same lineage of satirical management laws.

whyItMatters: It named, memorably, a widespread cynicism about corporate hierarchy, and the book that expanded it became a runaway bestseller — a sign of how deeply its caricature of office life resonated. As commentary it endures as a sharp, quotable foil to earnest management theory, even though it makes no claim to being one.

working.text: take the principle as a pointed joke about corporate incentives, not as a validated account of how promotion works.
use it against the Peter principle to see two cynical routes to the same end — incompetent managers — by opposite mechanisms.
note the genuine frustration it channels, that the people doing the work are not always the ones being promoted.

limits: It is satire and humour, an observational quip, not an empirically established management law; Scott Adams himself framed it as satire. It should be read as cultural commentary rather than a validated finding, and there is no body of evidence establishing that firms systematically promote their worst employees on purpose. What academic engagement exists — such as the computational study of random promotion strategies — addresses the Peter principle directly and is only thematically adjacent, not a validation of Adams's coinage.
misreadings: It is not a serious, tested theory of organisations but a comic exaggeration; treating it as documented fact mistakes a joke for data. And it is not the Peter principle: that promotes the competent until they fail, while the Dilbert principle promotes the incompetent up front, to sideline them — opposite mechanisms reaching the same cynical destination.
origin: Coined by Scott Adams, creator of the Dilbert comic strip, in a 1995 Wall Street Journal column and expanded into his 1996 bestseller 'The Dilbert Principle'; it plays off Laurence Peter's 1969 Peter principle and the earlier Putt's Law.

sources.text: Dilbert principle, Wikipedia. — the promote-the-incompetent-to-management statement, the 1995 column and 1996 book, and the contrast with the Peter principle.
Peter principle, Wikipedia. — the rise-to-the-level-of-incompetence idea the Dilbert principle inverts.
